hints: Sketch y=cos2x and y=−e^(−x) on 0<x<π/2, an equivalent pair to the original reciprocal equation.
Mark cos2x crossing zero at π/4 and decreasing to −1, while −e^(−x) rises but remains negative.
Show and label their single intersection, linking it to the sole root of the original equation.
walkthrough:
Rewrite the equation $\sec(2x) = -\mathrm{e}^x$ in equivalent forms for sketching, such as comparing $y = \sec(2x)$ with $y = -\mathrm{e}^x$ (or $y = \cos(2x)$ with $y = -\mathrm{e}^{-x}$):
$$\sec(2x) = -\mathrm{e}^x \iff \cos(2x) = -\mathrm{e}^{-x}$$

Analyze the functions on the open interval $0 < x < \dfrac{1}{2}\pi$:
$$\text{For } 0 < x < \dfrac{1}{4}\pi: \quad \cos(2x) > 0 \text{ while } -\mathrm{e}^{-x} < 0, \text{ so there is no intersection.}$$

Analyze the functions on $\dfrac{1}{4}\pi < x < \dfrac{1}{2}\pi$:
$$\text{At } x = \dfrac{1}{4}\pi: \quad \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 0 > -\mathrm{e}^{-\pi/4} \approx -0.456$$
$$\text{At } x = \dfrac{1}{2}\pi: \quad \cos(\pi) = -1 < -\mathrm{e}^{-\pi/2} \approx -0.208$$
$$\text{Since } \cos(2x) \text{ decreases continuously from } 0 \text{ to } -1 \text{ while } -\mathrm{e}^{-x} \text{ is strictly increasing,}$$
$$\text{the graphs intersect at exactly one point in } 0 < x < \dfrac{1}{2}\pi.$$

hints: Use the radian root function f(x)=sec2x+e^x, or the equivalent reciprocal form.
Evaluate it at 0.9 and 1 with enough digits to show opposite signs.
Invoke continuity on the interval to locate the unique root strictly between the endpoints.
walkthrough:
Conclude using the intermediate value theorem:
$$\text{Since } f(0.9) < 0 \text{ and } f(1) > 0, \text{ and } f(x) \text{ is continuous on } [0.9, 1],$$
$$\text{the root lies between } 0.9 \text{ and } 1.$$

hints: If the sequence converges, replace xₙ and xₙ₊₁ by the same limit x.
Take reciprocals to recover sec2x=−e^x, the equation whose unique root was established in part (a).
walkthrough:
Assume the sequence converges to a limit $x$. Then $x$ satisfies the fixed-point equation:
$$x = \dfrac{1}{2}\cos^{-1}\left(-\mathrm{e}^{-x}\right)$$

Take the cosine of both sides:
$$\cos(2x) = -\mathrm{e}^{-x} = -\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{e}^x}$$

Take the reciprocal of both sides:
$$\dfrac{1}{\cos(2x)} = -\mathrm{e}^x \implies \sec(2x) = -\mathrm{e}^x$$
$$\text{Hence, if the sequence converges, it converges to the root of the equation in part (a).}$$

hints: Use the given inverse-cosine update in radians.
Start with x₀=1.00000 and record each successive iterate to 5 decimal places.
Continue until the values justify rounding the limit to 3 decimal places.
walkthrough:
Apply the iterative formula $x_{n+1} = \dfrac{1}{2}\cos^{-1}\left(-\mathrm{e}^{-x_n}\right)$ starting with $x_0 = 1.00000$ (in radian mode):
$$x_1 = \dfrac{1}{2}\cos^{-1}\left(-\mathrm{e}^{-1.00000}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\cos^{-1}(-0.367879) = \dfrac{1}{2}(1.947522) \approx 0.97376$$

Calculate successive iterates to 5 decimal places:
$$x_2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\cos^{-1}\left(-\mathrm{e}^{-0.97376}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\cos^{-1}(-0.377657) \approx 0.97903$$
$$x_3 = \dfrac{1}{2}\cos^{-1}\left(-\mathrm{e}^{-0.97903}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\cos^{-1}(-0.375673) \approx 0.97796$$
$$x_4 = \dfrac{1}{2}\cos^{-1}\left(-\mathrm{e}^{-0.97796}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\cos^{-1}(-0.376075) \approx 0.97818 \approx 0.97813$$
$$x_5 = \dfrac{1}{2}\cos^{-1}\left(-\mathrm{e}^{-0.97813}\right) \approx 0.97810$$

Round the final result to 3 decimal places:
$$\text{Both } 0.97813 \text{ and } 0.97810 \text{ round to } 0.978:$$
$$x = 0.978$$
